title: Sunlight
shortHelp: How often the Sun rises above the local horizon, averaged over many years rather than for a chosen date.

source.name: LRO LOLA average solar illumination, south pole (AVGVISIB_65S_240M_201608)
source.citation: Mazarico, E., Neumann, G.A., Smith, D.E., Zuber, M.T., Torrence, M.H. (2011). Illumination conditions of the lunar polar regions using LOLA topography. Icarus 211(2), 1066-1081. doi:10.1016/j.icarus.2010.10.030
source.version: 201608 release (PDS label PRODUCT_VERSION_ID V1.05, created 2016-09-15), PDS dataset LRO-L-LOLA-4-GDR-V1.0 EXTRAS; 240 m/pixel

notes: Percent of hourly time steps in which any part of the Sun's disc is above the local horizon, simulated over ~18.6 years (one lunar nutation cycle) using LOLA 240 m topography (Mazarico et al. 2011, 2016 release). It is a long-term average, not a forecast for any date. Computed at ground level: a mast a few meters tall sees more Sun. Source pixels are 240 m, bilinearly resampled to ~297 m, so narrow ridge crests are smoothed and their peak values are underestimated. 0% = permanent shadow. Some faint linear artifacts come from the underlying DEM.

title: Earth in view
shortHelp: How often Earth is visible above the local horizon; visibility alone does not guarantee a working radio link.

source.name: LRO LOLA average Earth visibility, south pole (AVGVISIB_65S_240M_201608_EARTH)
source.citation: Mazarico, E., Neumann, G.A., Smith, D.E., Zuber, M.T., Torrence, M.H. (2011). Illumination conditions of the lunar polar regions using LOLA topography. Icarus 211(2), 1066-1081. doi:10.1016/j.icarus.2010.10.030
source.version: 201608 release (PDS label PRODUCT_VERSION_ID V1.05, created 2016-09-15), PDS dataset LRO-L-LOLA-4-GDR-V1.0 EXTRAS; 240 m/pixel

notes: Percent of hourly time steps in which any part of Earth's disc is above the local horizon, simulated over ~18.6 years from LOLA 240 m topography (same method and release as the Sunlight layer). Counting any sliver of Earth as 'visible' is a little optimistic, and it ignores which ground station on Earth is facing the Moon, so real direct-to-Earth contact time is lower. Long-term average at ground level, not a forecast; 240 m source resampled to ~297 m.

title: PSR
shortHelp: Permanently shadowed regions are cold traps where ice could survive; this older map does not show measured ice.

source.name: LRO LOLA permanently shadowed regions, south pole (LPSR_65S_240M_201608)
source.citation: Mazarico, E., Neumann, G.A., Smith, D.E., Zuber, M.T., Torrence, M.H. (2011). Illumination conditions of the lunar polar regions using LOLA topography. Icarus 211(2), 1066-1081. doi:10.1016/j.icarus.2010.10.030
source.version: 201608 release (PDS label PRODUCT_VERSION_ID V1.05, created 2016-09-15), PDS dataset LRO-L-LOLA-4-GDR-V1.0 EXTRAS; 240 m/pixel

notes: Published LOLA permanent-shadow map (never sunlit during the ~18.6-year simulation, Mazarico et al. 2011, 2016 release) - not derived by us. A permanently shadowed region is a cold trap where ice CAN be stable; this map does not prove ice is there (orbital evidence for surface ice is patchy). Nearest-neighbour resampled from 240 m to ~297 m, so shadows smaller than ~300 m can be missing or slightly misplaced.

title: Temperature
shortHelp: The hottest the ground gets during a year, modelled from NASA measurements rather than today’s temperature.

source.name: LRO Diviner Polar Resource Product, south pole (DLRE_PRP_SOUTH)
source.citation: Paige, D.A., et al. (2010). Diviner Lunar Radiometer observations of cold traps in the Moon's south polar region. Science 330(6003), 479-482. doi:10.1126/science.1187726. Dataset: Paige, D.A., LRO DLRE Level 5 Polar Resource Product V2.0, NASA Planetary Data System, LRO-L-DLRE-5-PRP-V2.0 (2018).

notes: Annual MAXIMUM surface temperature (PRP column temp_max). From a thermal model fitted to Diviner observations from LRO's first mapping year (2009-2010), computed on a ~0.5 km triangular mesh built from Kaguya laser altimetry (Paige et al. 2010). Linearly interpolated from triangle centres onto the ~297 m grid, so features smaller than ~1 km are blurred. Long-term model values, not today's temperature. Water ice can stay frozen for billions of years where it stays below about 110 K.

title: Average temperature
shortHelp: The modelled average temperature through a year, just below the ground.

source.name: LRO Diviner Polar Resource Product, south pole (DLRE_PRP_SOUTH)
source.citation: Paige, D.A., et al. (2010). Diviner Lunar Radiometer observations of cold traps in the Moon's south polar region. Science 330(6003), 479-482. doi:10.1126/science.1187726. Dataset: Paige, D.A., LRO DLRE Level 5 Polar Resource Product V2.0, NASA Planetary Data System, LRO-L-DLRE-5-PRP-V2.0 (2018).

notes: Annual AVERAGE temperature at 2 cm depth (PRP column temp_avg). An annual MINIMUM map is not published in this product, so we show the average instead. Where the average is below ~110 K, ice buried a little below the surface can be stable even if the surface gets warmer in summer. From a thermal model fitted to Diviner observations from LRO's first mapping year (2009-2010), computed on a ~0.5 km triangular mesh built from Kaguya laser altimetry (Paige et al. 2010). Linearly interpolated from triangle centres onto the ~297 m grid, so features smaller than ~1 km are blurred. Long-term model values, not today's temperature. Water ice can stay frozen for billions of years where it stays below about 110 K.

title: Slope
shortHelp: Slopes across the Moon, over about 1.4 km of ground; the south-pole map uses about 240 m.

source.name: NASA LOLA LDEM_64 global heights and LDEM_80S_80M south-pole heights
source.citation: Smith, D.E., et al. (2010). The Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter investigation on the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter mission. Space Science Reviews 150, 209-241. doi:10.1007/s11214-009-9512-y. Dataset: LRO LOLA Gridded Data Record, NASA Planetary Data System, LRO-L-LOLA-4-GDR-V1.0, product LDEM_80S_80M.
source.version: JP2 label PRODUCT_VERSION_ID V2.1 (IMG V2.0), created 2017-06-15; LOLA data 2009-07-13 to 2017-02-02

notes: Global slopes use NASA LOLA LDEM_64 heights and a local 3 by 3 ground stencil, about 1.42 km across. The south-pole map keeps the 80 m heights and about 240 m stencil. The 8192 by 4096 map is a resampling, not new detail. Small rocks and many driving hazards are unresolved.

title: Height colours
shortHelp: Colours show ground height: blue is low, red and white are high.

source.name: LRO LOLA polar digital elevation model LDEM_80S_80M (80 m/pixel)
source.citation: Smith, D.E., et al. (2010). The Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter investigation on the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter mission. Space Science Reviews 150, 209-241. doi:10.1007/s11214-009-9512-y. Dataset: LRO LOLA Gridded Data Record, NASA Planetary Data System, LRO-L-LOLA-4-GDR-V1.0, product LDEM_80S_80M.
source.version: JP2 label PRODUCT_VERSION_ID V2.1 (IMG V2.0), created 2017-06-15; LOLA data 2009-07-13 to 2017-02-02

notes: LOLA elevation relative to a 1737.4 km sphere (DN x 0.5 m), bilinearly resampled from 80 m to ~297 m pixels. The picture is coloured by height and shaded with an artificial light from the upper left (2x vertical exaggeration) - the shading is not real sunlight. Colours saturate at -6000 / +6000 m; click values give the true height.

title: PSR
shortHelp: Permanently shadowed regions never get direct sunlight; these cold traps could hold ice, but are not measured ice.

source.name: NASA LOLA permanent-shadow models, both poles; adjusted 20 m south-pole map
source.citation: Barker, M.K., Mazarico, E., Neumann, G.A., Smith, D.E., Zuber, M.T., Head, J.W., Sun, X. (2023). A New View of the Lunar South Pole from the Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA). The Planetary Science Journal 4, 183. doi:10.3847/PSJ/acf3e1. Data doi:10.60903/gsfcpgda-lola-spole.
source.version: PGDA product90; data DOI10.60903/gsfcpgda-lola-spole; primary TIFF Last-Modified2023-06-03

notes: LOLA permanent-shadow models poleward of 65 degrees at both poles. The north uses 240 m data, 120 m above 80 N and 60 m above 85 N. The south keeps its 20 m source in the same 4096-pixel picture, with 240 m coverage out to 65 S. Shadow is not a detection of ice.

title: Water ice
shortHelp: Purple shows hydrogen seen from orbit, not proven ice. Blue and cyan predict where ice could last. Only the white LCROSS ring marks water measured on the spot.
units: class: 0 none mapped; 1 predicted buried; 2 predicted surface; 3 orbital detection

source.name: NASA Diviner / LOLA cold-trap predictions; Lunar Prospector orbital hydrogen; crater-specific instrument evidence
source.citation: Paige, D.A., et al. (2010). Diviner Lunar Radiometer observations of cold traps in the Moon's south polar region. Science 330, 479-482. doi:10.1126/science.1187726. Dataset: Paige et al. (2018), LRO DLRE Level 5 PRP V2.0, NASA PDS, LRO-L-DLRE-5-PRP-V2.0. Barker, M.K., Mazarico, E., Neumann, G.A., Smith, D.E., Zuber, M.T., Head, J.W., Sun, X. (2023). A New View of the Lunar South Pole from the Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA). The Planetary Science Journal 4, 183. doi:10.3847/PSJ/acf3e1. Data doi:10.60903/gsfcpgda-lola-spole.
source.version: PRP V2.0 (2018-02-21), existing MOONDA temp-max linear grid; PGDA LOLA 20m PSR

notes: Purple is Lunar Prospector neutron-spectrometer hydrogen, in 0.5-degree bins with a much broader footprint; hydrogen can have causes other than ice. The spot value flags estimates of at least 100 ppm only as orbital signs, not ice. That threshold is a display choice. Blue and cyan are Diviner/LOLA cold-trap predictions, not detections. Only LCROSS measured water on the spot. Radar markers are candidates and can also be explained by rough ground.
coverage: Polar predictions; hydrogen across the Moon

units: 0 = no mapped warning; 1 = caution; 2 = steep; 3 = too steep to drive
